p: The Hebrew calls Doeg an Edomite; the Greek calls him a Syrian. The two words differ by one easily confused letter.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); KJV, NIV, ESV, BSB and almost all translations
Septuagint, the Greek translation made before Jesus (Rahlfs edition, following Codex Vaticanus, 300s AD)

why: In Hebrew script "Edomite" ('dmy) and "Aramean" ('rmy) differ only by the letters dalet and resh, which look almost alike and were often confused. The Hebrew reading is the same in 22:9, 22:18 and 22:22 and in the heading of Psalm 52, and Edomites were Saul's enemies (14:47), which suits a foreign herdsman in his service. The Plain English follows the Hebrew.
b: The Greek reads "Syrian" each time Doeg is named. Tov uses this pair of letters as a standard example of how scribes misread similar letters.

p: The Hebrew makes Doeg the head of Saul's shepherds; the Greek has him tending Saul's mules.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); KJV "the chiefest of the herdmen," modern translations
readings.en: the mightiest of the shepherds who belonged to Saul

readings.w: Septuagint, the Greek translation made before Jesus (Rahlfs edition, following Codex Vaticanus, 300s AD)

why: The Hebrew phrase is unusual (abbir usually means "mighty one," even "bull"), but it makes sense: Doeg was the strongest or chief of Saul's herdsmen. The Greek seems to have read or guessed a different Hebrew. Since the Hebrew is understandable and is the harder wording, the Plain English follows it.

a: He scratched marks on the doors of the gate
p: The Hebrew says David "made marks" on the gate doors; the Greek says he "drummed" on them.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008) (written wytw, read wytyw, "he made marks"); KJV "scrabbled," most modern translations
readings.en: he made marks on the doors of the gate
readings.plain: He scratched marks on the doors of the gate

readings.w: Septuagint, the Greek translation made before Jesus (Rahlfs edition, following Codex Vaticanus, 300s AD); adopted by some modern commentators
readings.orig: ἐτυμπάνιζεν ἐπὶ ταῖς θύραις τῆς πόλεως
readings.en: he drummed on the doors of the city
readings.plain: He drummed on the doors of the gate

why: The Greek "drummed" probably reflects a Hebrew wytp ("and he beat"), one letter different from the Hebrew wytw ("and he marked," from taw, a mark). Both fit a man acting mad. The Hebrew reading is supported by its own written and read forms (Ketiv and Qere), and the Plain English keeps it.

a: He brought them into the presence of the king of Moab
p: The Hebrew vowels say David brought his parents before the king of Moab. The same letters with other vowels say he left them there.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); KJV ("he brought them before the king of Moab")
readings.en: and he led them before the king of Moab
readings.plain: He brought them into the presence of the king of Moab

readings.w: Syriac, Targum and Vulgate, reading the same letters as vayyannichem; ESV, NIV and BSB ("he left them with the king of Moab")
readings.en: and he left them with the king of Moab
readings.plain: He left them with the king of Moab

why: The consonants are the same; only the vowels differ. Vayyanchem, "he led them," fits et-pene, "before the face of," the usual phrase for presenting someone to a king. Vayyannichem, "he left them," fits what happens next, since David returns to the stronghold. Either way David's parents stay in Moab under the king's protection. The Plain English keeps the Masoretic vowels, which make good sense.

t: Captain of the guard, or one who "turns aside" to it?
p: The Hebrew is awkward here. The Greek reads "commander," which most modern translations follow.

readings.w: Septuagint ("commander of all your orders"), presumed Hebrew behind the Greek reconstructed by modern scholars; with a small change of 'el to 'al; followed by the ESV, NIV and NRSV ("captain over your bodyguard")
readings.orig: וְשַׂר עַל־מִשְׁמַעְתֶּךָ / καὶ ἄρχων παντὸς παραγγέλματός σου

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); KJV "goeth at thy bidding"
readings.en: and one who turns aside to your bodyguard (or: your audience)
readings.plain: one who has access to your inner council

why: As pointed, the Hebrew sar el means "turns aside to," which is a strange way to describe David's post. The word for "captain" is also pronounced sar, but it is spelled with a different letter (sin instead of samekh). The two sounded alike, so a copyist could easily write one for the other, and the Greek translators seem to have had "captain" in front of them. Mishma'at means a royal bodyguard in 2 Samuel 23:23, and David had in fact been put in command of troops (18:13). The Plain English follows the reading behind the Greek, as McCarter and most modern translations do. The Hebrew can still be defended as meaning that David had special access to the king.

t: Eighty-five, or three hundred and five?
p: The Hebrew says Doeg killed 85 priests. The Greek says 305, and Josephus 385.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); KJV and modern translations
Septuagint, the Greek translation made before Jesus (Rahlfs edition, following Codex Vaticanus, 300s AD)
Josephus, Jewish Antiquities 6.260 (about AD 94)

why: Numbers are easily changed in copying, and no reason for either change is obvious. Josephus's 385 looks like a combination of the two others, which suggests that both 300 and 85 were known in his day. The Plain English follows the Hebrew, which is the only reading in a Hebrew manuscript; the larger number would fit a whole town of priests.

a: I have caused the loss of every life in your father's house
p: The Hebrew "I have turned" is hard. The Greek reads "I am to blame for the lives," which suggests a slightly different Hebrew word.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); Rashi and the KJV take it as "I have occasioned"
readings.en: I have brought it about against every life
readings.plain: I have caused the loss of every life in your father's house

readings.w: Septuagint, the Greek translation made before Jesus (Rahlfs edition, following Codex Vaticanus, 300s AD); followed by many modern commentators (reading Hebrew chavti, "I am guilty")
readings.en: I am responsible for the lives
readings.plain: I am to blame for the lives of everyone in your father's house

why: Sabboti, from "turn," is an odd form, but it can mean "I have turned (events) against" or "I have been the cause." The Greek seems to have read chavti, "I am guilty," a rare Aramaic-like word. The meaning hardly changes: David takes the blame. The Plain English keeps the Hebrew.

p: The written Hebrew has "your enemies"; the reading tradition has "your enemy."

readings.w: Masoretic reading tradition (Qere); KJV and modern translations
Masoretic written text (Ketiv)

why: The scribes who handed down the Hebrew text marked some words to be read differently from how they were written (Ketiv, "written," and Qere, "read"). Here the read form, "your enemy," fits the context, since only Saul is in the cave. The written plural may be a general saying ("I will give your enemies into your hand") that the men apply to Saul.

a: my eye took pity on you
p: The Hebrew verb has no stated subject. The Plain English supplies "my eye"; the Greek and Latin read "I spared you."

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008) (verb with no stated subject, completed as "my eye" by most commentators); KJV "mine eye spared thee"
readings.plain: my eye took pity on you

readings.w: Septuagint, the Greek translation made before Jesus (Rahlfs edition, following Codex Vaticanus, 300s AD); Targum; Vulgate; ESV ("but I spared you")

why: The Hebrew verb is feminine, "and she pitied you," with no subject. Hebrew often says "your eye shall not pity" (Deuteronomy 7:16; 13:8), and "eye" is feminine, so most commentators think "my eye" is understood or dropped out. The Greek, Targum and Latin smooth it to "I." The meaning is the same. The Plain English supplies "my eye" to keep the Hebrew idiom.

p: The Hebrew sends David to the far-off wilderness of Paran; the Greek has the nearby wilderness of Maon.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); KJV, ESV, NRSV, BSB
Septuagint, the Greek translation made before Jesus (Rahlfs edition, following Codex Vaticanus, 300s AD) ("Maan"); noted in the text or footnotes of several modern translations

why: Paran is the desert of the Sinai Peninsula where Israel wandered (Numbers 10:12), far south of the story's setting. Maon fits the next verse, which begins in Maon, and David had been in the wilderness of Maon before (23:24–25). But that is exactly why a scribe might have changed Paran to Maon. Paran is the harder reading, and it might be used loosely for the whole southern wilderness. The Plain English follows the Hebrew, with real doubt.

p: The read Hebrew says Nabal was a Calebite. The written form can be read "like his heart," and the Greek read the same letters as "doglike."

readings.w: Masoretic reading tradition (Qere); Targum; KJV and modern translations
Masoretic written text (Ketiv), read as kelibbo; no ancient translation follows it
readings.plain: He was a man who did as his heart pleased

readings.w: Septuagint (κυνικός, "doglike"), reading the consonants of the read form as kalbi, from kelev, "dog"

why: The read form, kalibbi, "Calebite," fits the setting: Caleb's clan held the land around Hebron and Maon (Joshua 14:13–14; 15:13). The written form klbw can be read kelibbo, "like his heart," that is, headstrong, but no ancient translation takes it that way. The Greek kynikos, "doglike," comes from the read form's letters klby, taken as kalbi, from kelev, "dog." Many readers think the narrator meant the pun: Nabal the Calebite is a dog. The Plain English follows the read form.

a: May God do this to David
t: A curse on David or on David's enemies?
p: The Hebrew says "May God do this to David's enemies." The Greek says "to David," and the Hebrew was probably softened by scribes.

readings.w: Septuagint, the Greek translation made before Jesus (Rahlfs edition, following Codex Vaticanus, 300s AD); adopted by most modern commentators and the NIV, NRSV and BSB
readings.orig: τάδε ποιήσαι ὁ θεὸς τῷ Δαυιδ
readings.en: May God do so to David
readings.plain: May God do this to David

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); KJV, ESV
readings.en: May God do so to the enemies of David
readings.plain: May God do this to David's enemies

why: An oath of this kind always calls a curse down on the speaker if he fails to keep it (3:17; 14:44; 20:13). A curse on "David's enemies" makes no sense in David's own mouth. Since David does not carry out his oath, scribes seem to have added "enemies" so that the curse would not fall on him, a known kind of reverent correction. The same softening appears in 20:16 and 2 Samuel 12:14. The Plain English follows the Greek, which preserves the older wording.

p: The Hebrew repeats the flea from 24:14; the Greek reads "to seek my life."

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); KJV, ESV, NIV
Septuagint, the Greek translation made before Jesus (Rahlfs edition, following Codex Vaticanus, 300s AD); followed by some commentators

why: The Greek may preserve an original "to seek my life" (a common phrase in these chapters, 20:1; 22:23; 23:15; 25:29), with the Hebrew borrowing the flea from 24:14. But the flea also fits here, next to the partridge, and a translator could easily replace an odd image with a common phrase. The Plain English keeps the Hebrew.

t: "The king's spear" or "the spear, O king"?
p: The written Hebrew reads "Here is the spear, O king"; the reading tradition has "Here is the king's spear."

readings.w: Masoretic reading tradition (Qere); KJV and most translations
Masoretic written text (Ketiv)
readings.en: Here is the spear, O king
readings.plain: Look, here is the spear, O king!

why: The written form adds the article to "spear," which turns "the king" into a form of address. Both readings make sense. The read form is the usual one and the Plain English follows it; the written form would have David speak to Saul directly, as he does in 26:17.

p: The written Hebrew has Girzites, an unknown people; the read form has Gizrites, perhaps people of Gezer.

readings.w: Masoretic written text (Ketiv); NIV, ESV, BSB
Masoretic reading tradition (Qere); KJV "the Gezrites"

why: Gezer, the city the read form seems to point to, lay far to the north, near the Philistine plain, not in the southern desert between Shur and Egypt where these raids took place. The written form names a people otherwise unknown, which is the harder reading and more likely to be original. The Greek of this verse differs again and lists the peoples differently.

p: The Hebrew says the peoples lived there "from of old." The Greek has a place name here, often taken as Telam.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); KJV, ESV, NIV

Septuagint, the Greek translation made before Jesus (Rahlfs edition, following Codex Vaticanus, 300s AD) (Γελαμψουρ, usually explained as "from Telam to Shur"); adopted by McCarter and other commentators

why: The Hebrew asher me'olam, "which from of old," is awkward after "the land." The Greek seems to have read mitTelam, "from Telam," a town in the far south where Saul mustered his army against Amalek (15:4, Telaim; Joshua 15:24). The letters of the two readings are close. The Greek gives a neat border description, from Telam to Shur, and many commentators adopt it. The Plain English keeps the Hebrew because it makes sense as it stands. 4QSam-a preserves parts of this verse (as listed in DJD 17), but its reading here is not reported in the works used for this edition.

p: The Hebrew begins Achish's question with a puzzling word. The Greek reads "against whom."

readings.w: Septuagint, the Greek translation made before Jesus (Rahlfs edition, following Codex Vaticanus, 300s AD) (ἐπὶ τίνα); Vulgate (In quem irruistis hodie?, "Against whom did you rush in today?"); followed by the NRSV and, loosely, the BSB ("What have you raided today?")
readings.en: Against whom did you make a raid today?

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008) ('al), as understood by some medieval Jewish commentators, the KJV ("Whither have ye made a road to day?"), the ESV and the NIV

why: The Hebrew 'al usually means "do not," which makes no sense here. Some medieval commentators explained it as "where," but that meaning is found nowhere else. The Greek and the Latin both read "against whom," which suggests a Hebrew 'el mi, from which one short word could easily drop out. 4QSam-a preserves parts of 27:8–12 (as listed in DJD 17), but its reading at this word is not reported in the works used here. The Plain English follows the Greek and Latin; the sense is almost the same either way.

p: The Hebrew has Achish say David will march out "in the camp"; the Greek says "to battle."

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); ESV, World English Bible ("in the army")
readings.en: you will go out with me in the camp

readings.w: Septuagint, the Greek translation made before Jesus (Rahlfs edition, following Codex Vaticanus, 300s AD); KJV and BSB ("to battle"), perhaps as a free rendering
readings.en: you will go out with me to war

why: Both readings make sense, and the difference is small (bammachaneh, "in the camp," against lammilchamah, "to battle"). The Greek may have read the more expected phrase, or may preserve it; the Hebrew uses "camp" for the army again in 28:5 and 29:6. The Plain English keeps the Hebrew.

p: The Hebrew and Greek say the Philistines gathered to fight Israel. The Dead Sea Scroll 4QSam-a is reported to read "at Jezreel."

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); Septuagint; KJV and modern translations
4QSam-a (Dead Sea Scroll, Cave 4, 1st century BC), as reported by Ulrich and in the Dead Sea Scrolls Bible (reconstruction in DJD 17 not checked here)
readings.orig: יזרעאלה (the scroll's word for the place, as reported)

why: In Hebrew, Yisra'el (Israel) and Yizre'el (Jezreel) differ by one letter and sound alike. The scroll's reading names the battlefield, matching 29:1 and 29:11, where the Philistines go up to Jezreel. A copyist could have changed either name into the other: "Israel" is the far more common word, but "to fight Israel" is also the usual phrase. Because the scroll's text here is fragmentary and is known to this edition only from reports, the Plain English keeps the reading of the Hebrew and Greek, which say the same thing in general terms.

p: The Hebrew word for "your foe" is rare. The Greek reads "and has gone over to your neighbor," which matches the next verse.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); KJV, ESV, NIV
Septuagint, the Greek translation made before Jesus (Rahlfs edition, following Codex Vaticanus, 300s AD); followed by some commentators
readings.orig: καὶ γέγονεν μετὰ τοῦ πλησίον σου
readings.en: and has come to be with your neighbor

why: 'Ar, "foe," is a rare word known mainly from Aramaic (Daniel 4:19), and it is spelled here like 'arekha. The Greek seems to have read re'ekha, "your neighbor," the word used in 28:17 for David. A scribe may have harmonized one verse to the other in either direction. The Hebrew is the harder reading, and the Plain English follows it.

a: The LORD has done to you
p: The Hebrew says the LORD has done this "to him" or "for himself." The Greek, Latin and some Hebrew manuscripts say "to you."

readings.w: Septuagint, the Greek translation made before Jesus (Rahlfs edition, following Codex Vaticanus, 300s AD); Latin Vulgate (tibi); some Hebrew manuscripts; ESV, NRSV
readings.en: The LORD has done to you
readings.plain: The LORD has done to you

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008) (lo); KJV "to him"
readings.en: The LORD has done for himself (or: to him)
readings.plain: The LORD has done for himself

why: "To him" is hard to explain: it might mean "for himself," for God's own purpose, or "to David," mentioned only at the end of the verse. "To you" (lekha) fits Samuel's speech, which is addressed to Saul throughout (28:16, 18), and it is supported by two independent ancient translations. The Plain English follows "to you," but the Hebrew may preserve the harder, original wording.

p: The Greek has "Aendor" here, the same place as the medium's town. It is probably a misreading of the Hebrew for "at the spring."

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); KJV and modern translations
readings.en: at the spring which is in Jezreel

readings.w: Septuagint, the Greek translation made before Jesus (Rahlfs edition, following Codex Vaticanus, 300s AD)
readings.en: at Aendor, which is in Jezreel

why: The Hebrew ba'ayin, "at the spring," begins like the place name En-dor ('en dor, "spring of Dor"), and a copyist or translator seems to have been thinking of chapter 28. Endor lay north of the Philistine camp, not by Israel's camp at the foot of Gilboa, so the Hebrew fits the geography. The Plain English follows it.

a: Go to the place where I stationed you, and do not take any evil word to heart, for in my eyes you are good.
t: A sentence lost from the Hebrew?
p: The Greek has a sentence the Hebrew lacks. A copyist's eye probably skipped from one "rise early" to the next.

readings.w: Septuagint, the Greek translation made before Jesus (Rahlfs edition, following Codex Vaticanus, 300s AD); followed by the NRSV and some commentators
readings.orig: καὶ πορεύεσθε εἰς τὸν τόπον οὗ κατέστησα ὑμᾶς ἐκεῖ, καὶ λόγον λοιμὸν μὴ θῇς ἐν καρδίᾳ σου, ὅτι ἀγαθὸς σὺ ἐνώπιόν μου
readings.en: and go to the place where I appointed you, and do not set a harmful word in your heart, for you are good in my sight
readings.plain: Go to the place where I stationed you, and do not take any evil word to heart, for in my eyes you are good.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); KJV, ESV, NIV, BSB

why: In the Hebrew, Achish says "rise early" twice in one breath. In the Greek, the extra sentence comes between the two. That is the classic setting for a copyist's slip: his eye jumped from the first "rise early" to the second, and the words between were lost (haplography). The sentence also fits Achish's gentle tone and his words "to the place you put him" (29:4). The Plain English includes it, following the Greek, though without a Hebrew witness it remains uncertain.
b: Scholars who prefer the shorter Hebrew note that a translator could have expanded Achish's speech to soften his dismissal of David. The longer text appears in the NRSV.

a: the women who were in it
p: The Hebrew says the raiders took the women captive. The Greek says "the women and everyone" in the town.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); KJV
readings.en: the women who were in it
readings.plain: the women who were in it

readings.w: Septuagint, the Greek translation made before Jesus (Rahlfs edition, following Codex Vaticanus, 300s AD); ESV, NIV, NRSV and BSB ("the women and all who were in it")
readings.orig: τὰς γυναῖκας καὶ πάντα τὰ ἐν αὐτῇ
readings.en: the women and everything that was in it
readings.plain: the women and everyone who was in it

why: The Greek may preserve the words "and all" (ve'et-kol), lost when a copyist's eye skipped. Or it may have filled out the phrase, since 30:3 and 30:19 show that sons and daughters were taken too. The Hebrew as it stands, "the women ... from the youngest to the oldest," makes sense and the next verses supply the children. 4QSam-a is not preserved at this verse, so the Greek is the only witness for the longer text. The Plain English follows the Hebrew.

p: The Hebrew sends gifts to "Bethel." The Greek has Beth-zur, a town in the hills of Judah.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); KJV and modern translations
Septuagint, the Greek translation made before Jesus (Rahlfs edition, following Codex Vaticanus, 300s AD) (Βαιθσουρ)

why: The famous Bethel lay far to the north in Benjamin, so many think the Hebrew means a southern town called Bethuel or Bethul (Joshua 19:4; 1 Chronicles 4:30). The Greek's Beth-zur (Joshua 15:58), north of Hebron, is a known town of Judah and may be the translators' guess for a name they did not know, or the better text. The Greek list in 30:27–30 differs in several names and adds towns in 30:28. 4QSam-a preserves parts of 30:22–31 (as listed in DJD 17), but its readings in the town list are not reported in the works used here. The Plain English keeps the Hebrew.

p: The Hebrew names an otherwise unknown town, Racal. The Greek has Carmel, Nabal and Abigail's town.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); KJV and modern translations
Septuagint, the Greek translation made before Jesus (Rahlfs edition, following Codex Vaticanus, 300s AD) (Καρμηλος); adopted by McCarter

why: Racal appears nowhere else. Carmel, just north of Maon, is where Nabal kept his flocks (25:2), and David had married into that community, so a gift there makes sense. The letters of the two names overlap (rkl and krml), and the Greek may preserve the original. But an unknown name is not proof of an error, and the Hebrew is the harder reading. The Plain English keeps "Racal" and notes that "Carmel" is a strong alternative.

p: The Leningrad Codex reads Bor-ashan; the printed Hebrew Bible behind the KJV read Chor-ashan.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); most modern translations
Other Hebrew manuscripts and the printed Rabbinic Bible of 1524–25; KJV "Chorashan"

why: The two Hebrew letters bet and kaf are very similar. The town is probably the Ashan of Joshua 15:42 and 19:7, in the lowlands of Judah, later given to Simeon. "Bor" means "pit" or "well," "Cor" means "furnace"; both suit "smoke" (ashan). The Plain English follows the oldest complete manuscript.
